quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten checks on process costing, equivalent units and work in process.

questions.q: Process costing assigns costs by
options: Tracing every cost to a specific customer order
Using broad averages over masses of similar units
Charging all cost to the last unit produced
questions.explain: Identical items mass-produced for general sale are costed by averaging; tracing to a specific order is job costing.

questions.q: The principal difference between job and process costing is
questions.explain: Jobs use different quantities of resources so each is costed separately; like units mass-produced are averaged over all units produced.

questions.q: In the Sino-Pak example, conversion cost includes
options: Labour, indirect materials, energy and plant depreciation
questions.explain: The example uses one direct-cost category (direct materials); everything else needed to convert cotton to yarn is grouped as conversion cost.

questions.q: An equivalent unit is
options: A fraction of a whole unit representing the work actually done on part-finished units
questions.explain: 1,000 bags 60 % complete as to conversion are 600 equivalent units of conversion work, though they are 1,000 physical units.

questions.q: In the Sino-Pak example, direct materials are added at the start of the process, so ending WIP is 100 % complete as to materials.
questions.explain: Materials go in at the start, so every bag in process already carries its full material; only conversion is partly done.

questions.q: Why is dividing February's Rs 29,200,000 by 6,000 physical bags wrong?
options: Because 6,000 is the wrong physical count
Because the unfinished bags have not yet absorbed all their conversion cost
Because the cost should be divided by 5,000
questions.explain: The 1,000 bags in process received only 60 % of their conversion work, so the cost must be spread over equivalent units, not physical units.

questions.q: Case I needs no equivalent-unit calculation because
options: There is no beginning or ending work in process
questions.explain: With every bag started and completed in January, physical units and equivalent units are the same — 6,000.

questions.q: The weighted-average method
options: Costs only the current period's work
Pools the opening WIP cost with the cost added this period
questions.explain: Weighted average blends the beginning WIP cost with March's cost and divides by total equivalent units; the current-period-only view is FIFO.

questions.q: The FIFO view of March uses more equivalent units than the weighted-average view.
questions.explain: FIFO deducts the beginning WIP equivalents (1,000 materials, 600 conversion) to count only March's own work: 5,500 and 5,650, fewer than the weighted-average 6,500 and 6,250.

questions.q: Which product is most suited to process costing?
options: A continuously spun Ne 20/1 yarn for stock
questions.explain: The yarn is identical and mass-produced for general sale; the others are distinct jobs with different resource use.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The equivalent-unit arithmetic and how the figures move when completion percentages or costs change.

questions.q: Equivalent units of conversion for ending WIP are
options: Physical units in WIP × % complete as to conversion
questions.explain: 1,000 bags × 60 % = 600 equivalent units in February; the physical count on its own overstates the conversion work done.

questions.q: Cost per equivalent unit of conversion is
options: Conversion cost ÷ equivalent units of conversion
Total cost ÷ equivalent units of materials
questions.explain: Rs 11,200,000 ÷ 5,600 = Rs 2,000 per bag in February; dividing by 6,000 started or 5,000 completed gives the wrong unit cost.

questions.q: Cost of ending WIP equals
options: Physical WIP units × average cost per completed bag
Materials EU × materials cost per EU + conversion EU × conversion cost per EU
Physical WIP units × conversion cost per EU
questions.explain: February: 1,000 × 3,000 + 600 × 2,000 = Rs 4,200,000. Using the full Rs 5,000 per bag (Rs 5,000,000) overstates the unfinished work.

questions.q: If the ending WIP were 80 % complete as to conversion instead of 60 %, the conversion cost per equivalent unit (with the same cost) would fall.
questions.explain: Equivalent units would rise from 5,600 to 5,800, and the same Rs 11,200,000 spread over more units gives a lower cost per unit (about Rs 1,931).

questions.q: Under the weighted-average method, total cost to account for equals
options: Beginning WIP cost + cost added this period
Ending WIP cost + beginning WIP cost
questions.explain: March: 4,200,000 of opening cost + 27,800,000 added = Rs 32,000,000, which is then split between bags transferred out and ending WIP.

questions.q: The FIFO equivalent units for the current period are found by
options: Adding beginning WIP equivalents to the weighted-average figure
Subtracting beginning WIP equivalents from the weighted-average figure
questions.explain: 6,500 − 1,000 = 5,500 materials and 6,250 − 600 = 5,650 conversion for March's own work.

questions.q: Cost of bags transferred out under weighted average equals
options: Bags completed × (materials cost per EU + conversion cost per EU)
Bags completed × materials cost per EU
questions.explain: 6,000 × (3,000 + 2,000) = Rs 30,000,000 in March; each completed bag carries both its material and its full conversion cost.

questions.q: Weighted-average and FIFO unit costs are always identical.
questions.explain: They coincided in March only because costs per unit were stable (3,000 and 2,000 both periods); if March's costs had differed from the opening WIP costs, the two methods would give different unit costs.

questions.q: Physical units to account for in a period equal
questions.explain: March: 1,000 + 5,500 = 6,500 physical bags, which must equal 6,000 completed + 500 in ending WIP.

questions.q: If conversion cost per equivalent unit rises while materials cost is unchanged, the average cost per completed bag
questions.explain: Average cost per completed bag is the sum of the two unit costs, so a higher conversion unit cost raises it.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Recompute the January, February and March sheets of Sino-Pak Textiles and extend them.

questions.q: In January 6,000 bags were started and completed with direct materials Rs 18,000,000 and conversion Rs 12,000,000. Average cost per bag?
questions.explain: Total 30,000,000 ÷ 6,000 = Rs 5,000 per bag (3,000 materials + 2,000 conversion).

questions.q: In February 5,000 bags were completed and 1,000 remain in process 60 % complete as to conversion. Equivalent units of conversion?
questions.explain: 5,000 + 1,000 × 0.6 = 5,600 equivalent units.

questions.q: February conversion cost added was Rs 11,200,000 over 5,600 equivalent units. Conversion cost per equivalent unit?
questions.explain: 11,200,000 ÷ 5,600 = Rs 2,000 per equivalent unit.

questions.q: Ending WIP of 1,000 bags is 100 % complete for materials (Rs 3,000 per EU) and 60 % complete for conversion (Rs 2,000 per EU). Cost of ending WIP?
In February 5,000 bags were transferred out at Rs 3,000 materials and Rs 2,000 conversion per bag. Cost of bags transferred out?
questions.explain: 5,000 × 5,000 = Rs 25,000,000; with ending WIP 4,200,000 this accounts for the full 29,200,000.

questions.q: March: 6,000 bags completed and 500 in ending WIP, 50 % complete as to conversion. Weighted-average equivalent units of conversion?
questions.explain: 6,000 + 250 = 6,250 equivalent units.

questions.q: March total conversion cost to account for is Rs 12,500,000 (Rs 1,200,000 in beginning WIP plus Rs 11,300,000 added) over 6,250 equivalent units. Weighted-average conversion cost per EU?
questions.explain: 12,500,000 ÷ 6,250 = Rs 2,000 per equivalent unit.

questions.q: Under FIFO, March's own work in conversion is 6,250 weighted-average EU minus 600 EU in beginning WIP. If Rs 11,300,000 was added in March, what is the FIFO conversion cost per EU?
questions.explain: 11,300,000 ÷ 5,650 = Rs 2,000 — the same as weighted average because costs were stable.

questions.q: March ending WIP: 500 bags, materials 100 % at Rs 3,000 and conversion 50 % at Rs 2,000 per EU. Its cost is
If February's Rs 29,200,000 were divided by 6,000 physical bags, the cost per bag (to the nearest rupee) would be
questions.explain: 29,200,000 ÷ 6,000 = Rs 4,867, below the true Rs 5,000 because the unfinished bags have not absorbed all their conversion cost.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Mill situations where process costing and equivalent units change the reported cost.

questions.q: A spinning mill makes only Ne 20/1 for stock, around the clock. The costing office should treat each month's output as
options: One process, averaging cost over equivalent units
questions.explain: Identical yarn mass-produced for general sale is the textbook case for process costing; job cards per bag or shift would be pointless effort.

questions.q: At month end the floor supervisor reports 1,000 bags 'in process' but cannot say how complete they are. The costing office
options: Can finish the sheet without this figure
Must estimate the % completion for conversion to compute equivalent units
Should count them as fully complete
questions.explain: Equivalent units of conversion depend on the degree of completion; without it, the split between transferred-out cost and WIP cost cannot be made.

questions.q: The supervisor overstates WIP completion as 80 % when it is really 60 %. The effect on February's conversion cost per EU is
questions.explain: More equivalent units (5,800 instead of 5,600) for the same cost gives a lower unit cost, so completed bags are undercosted and WIP overvalued.

questions.q: If the mill also started spinning Ne 30/1 on separate frames, a single average cost per bag across both counts would be appropriate.
questions.explain: Averaging is right only for like units; different counts use different quantities of resources, so each should be costed as its own process (or line).

questions.q: A mill completed 4,000 bags in April and has 800 bags in ending WIP, 25 % converted, with no beginning WIP. Conversion cost was Rs 8,400,000. What is the conversion cost per equivalent unit?
The finance manager asks for the value of yarn in process at month end for the balance sheet. The correct figure is
options: Physical bags × average cost per completed bag
Materials EU × materials unit cost + conversion EU × conversion unit cost
Zero, because the bags are unfinished
questions.explain: Ending WIP is valued at the work actually done on it — Rs 4,200,000 in February, not 1,000 × 5,000 = Rs 5,000,000.

questions.q: Cotton prices jumped in March, so March's material cost per bag is higher than the opening WIP's. A manager wants the unit cost to reflect only March's buying. Which method suits?
options: FIFO (work done in the current period only)
questions.explain: FIFO divides only March's cost by March's own equivalent units, isolating the current period; weighted average blends in the older, cheaper opening cost.

questions.q: A mill started 7,000 bags with no beginning WIP, completed 6,200 and left 800 in process. Materials (added at the start) cost Rs 21,000,000. Materials cost per equivalent unit?
questions.explain: All 7,000 bags are 100 % complete for materials, so EU = 7,000 and 21,000,000 ÷ 7,000 = Rs 3,000.

questions.q: A dyeing plant that processes many small custom lots asks whether to switch from job costing to process costing to save clerical work. Your advice is
options: Switch — averaging is always simpler and accurate
Do not switch — lots use different resources, so an average would miscost them
questions.explain: The lecture's rule: averaging is right only when like units are mass-produced; distinct lots with different resource use need job costing.

questions.q: A mill's February sheet shows cost per EU of Rs 3,000 materials and Rs 2,000 conversion, and transfers 5,000 bags out. The amount moved to finished goods inventory is

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Two-step problems, FIFO versus weighted average, and the common slips in process costing.

questions.q: March: beginning WIP 1,000 bags (materials Rs 3,000,000, conversion Rs 1,200,000); started 5,500; completed 6,000; ending WIP 500 at 50 % conversion. Materials added Rs 16,500,000 and conversion added Rs 11,300,000. Total cost to account for?
questions.explain: 4,200,000 opening + 27,800,000 added = Rs 32,000,000, which splits into 30,000,000 transferred out and 2,000,000 ending WIP.

questions.q: March weighted-average equivalent units of materials are 6,500 and beginning WIP held 1,000 bags fully complete for materials. How many equivalent units of materials did March's own work (FIFO) cover?
questions.explain: 6,500 − 1,000 = 5,500, equal to the bags started in March since materials are added at the start.

questions.q: A student values February's ending WIP at Rs 5,000,000. Their mistake is
options: Using 1,000 physical bags × Rs 5,000 instead of equivalent units
questions.explain: WIP has full materials (3,000,000) but only 60 % conversion (600 × 2,000 = 1,200,000), so Rs 4,200,000; charging full conversion overstates it by Rs 800,000.

questions.q: Suppose March's conversion cost added had been Rs 12,430,000 instead of Rs 11,300,000, with FIFO equivalent units of 5,650. What is the FIFO conversion cost per EU?
questions.explain: 12,430,000 ÷ 5,650 = Rs 2,200 — FIFO shows the cost increase in full, whereas weighted average would blend it with the Rs 2,000 opening cost.

questions.q: Using the figures of the previous question (conversion added Rs 12,430,000; opening WIP conversion Rs 1,200,000; weighted-average conversion EU 6,250), what is the weighted-average conversion cost per EU? Give to the nearest rupee.
questions.explain: 13,630,000 ÷ 6,250 = Rs 2,180.8 ≈ Rs 2,181, lower than FIFO's Rs 2,200 because the cheaper opening cost is pooled in.

questions.q: In March, physical units completed (6,000) plus ending WIP (500) must equal beginning WIP (1,000) plus units started (5,500).
questions.explain: The physical flow must balance: 6,500 bags to account for and 6,500 accounted for. Checking this first catches many data errors.

questions.q: Why were weighted-average and FIFO unit costs identical in March (Rs 3,000 and Rs 2,000)?
options: Because there was no ending WIP
Because the opening WIP cost per EU equalled March's cost per EU
Because materials were added at the end
questions.explain: Opening WIP carried 3,000 and 2,000 per EU (3,000,000 ÷ 1,000 and 1,200,000 ÷ 600), the same as March's own rates, so pooling changed nothing.

questions.q: A mill has 2,000 bags in ending WIP that are 100 % complete for materials and 30 % for conversion. Unit costs are Rs 3,100 materials and Rs 2,050 conversion. Value of the ending WIP?
If materials were added at the END of the process instead of the start, February's equivalent units of materials would be
questions.explain: The 1,000 unfinished bags would have received no materials yet, so only the 5,000 completed bags count — and the material cost per EU would rise to Rs 3,600.

questions.q: The weighted-average cost per EU in March came to Rs 5,000 per bag. The cost transferred out was
questions.explain: 6,000 completed bags × Rs 5,000 = Rs 30,000,000. Rs 32,000,000 is the total to account for including the ending WIP; 32,500,000 wrongly multiplies by the 6,500 physical units.
